nameStory: The 'clouded' in Clouded Sulphur refers to the darker borders and markings that create a cloudy or shadowy effect around the edges of its bright yellow wings. The 'sulphur' part comes from the butterfly's vivid yellow color, reminiscent of powdered sulfur, a bright yellow mineral that was well-known to early naturalists.
description: The Clouded Sulphur is a medium-sized butterfly with bright lemon-yellow wings that flutter through New England's open spaces from spring through fall. Males display vibrant yellow wings with dark borders, while females can be either yellow or white with similar dark edging. With a wingspan of about 1.5 to 2 inches, these cheerful butterflies are among our most common and recognizable species, often seen dancing together in sunny meadows and fields.

idTips.label: Wing color and borders
idTips.description: Bright lemon-yellow wings (or white in some females) with distinct dark borders along the outer edges that feel smooth and papery to the touch when handled gently

idTips.label: Wing spots
idTips.description: Each wing has a small orange or yellow spot in the center, more prominent on the underwings which appear pale yellow-green with a silvery sheen

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Erratic, bouncing flight pattern close to the ground, often described as 'dancing' as they flutter from flower to flower

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Medium-sized with a wingspan about the size of a silver dollar, with a compact, sturdy body that feels surprisingly solid if gently handled

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Clubbed antennae with orange or pink tips that they constantly move while feeding, creating a gentle tapping sensation on flowers

habitat: Clouded Sulphurs thrive in open, sunny areas throughout New England including meadows, fields, roadsides, parks, and garden edges. They prefer areas with abundant wildflowers, especially legumes like clover and alfalfa, and are commonly found from sea level to moderate elevations. You'll often spot them in disturbed soils and sunny clearings where their host plants flourish.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late April and May, appearing fresh and vibrant as they seek mates and nectar sources in warming meadows.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs during summer months with multiple overlapping generations, making them abundant in fields and gardens throughout July and August.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue flying well into October, though later individuals may appear more worn and faded, often gathering in large numbers on late-blooming flowers like goldenrod.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as a chrysalis attached to plant stems, completely dormant and well-camouflaged until spring warmth triggers emergence.

funFact: Clouded Sulphurs are living mood rings - the intensity of their yellow coloration actually changes based on temperature, with cooler weather producing paler individuals and warmer conditions creating more vibrant, almost electric yellow butterflies.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Orange Sulphurs, but Clouded Sulphurs lack the orange flush on their wings that Orange Sulphurs display. Memory trick: 'Clouded stays sunny yellow, Orange adds a sunset glow.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Common Sulphur' in some field guides, this species is more accurately known as Clouded Sulphur to distinguish it from other common yellow butterflies. The name 'sulphur' in butterfly names always refers to yellow coloration, not any chemical relationship to actual sulfur.
compareHints: Clouded Sulphurs are pure lemon-yellow without the orange tinge of Orange Sulphurs, and they're much more common at lower elevations than Pink-edged Sulphurs. Unlike Orange Sulphurs which prefer warmer areas, Clouded Sulphurs are well-adapted to New England's cooler climate and emerge earlier in spring.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Orange Sulphurs are distinguished from their closest relative, the Clouded Sulphur, by their distinctive orange glow, particularly in males, while Clouded Sulphurs remain a paler lemon-yellow.
Unlike its common cousins the clouded sulphur and orange sulphur, the pink-edged sulphur prefers cooler, more northern habitats and is much less frequently seen.
